Setup recipes in Swift and metal-cpp: device, queue, pipeline states loaded from a precompiled metallib, vertex descriptors, frames in flight gated by a semaphore, CAMetalLayer configuration (pixelFormat bgra8Unorm_srgb, maximumDrawableCount, displaySyncEnabled).

Storage modes and memory: shared (unified memory) vs private vs memoryless; heaps and aliasing; hazard-tracking modes; MTLFence/MTLEvent for untracked heaps; never use managed storage on Apple silicon.
Residency: resources reached only through argument buffers need useResource/useHeap (Metal 3) or an MTLResidencySet (macOS 15+/Metal 4). Missing residency produces garbage reads or GPU faults.
Argument buffers tier 2 for bindless: encoding gpuResourceID and gpuAddress, MSL struct declarations, arrays of textures, CPU-write synchronization with in-flight frames.

TBDR optimization: loadAction/storeAction per attachment (dontCare, clear), memoryless depth and MSAA targets, tile shaders and imageblocks for on-tile deferred, programmable blending via [[color(n)]] reads, raster order groups.

MSL vs HLSL/GLSL: address spaces (device/constant/threadgroup), [[buffer(n)]]/[[texture(n)]] attributes, half precision for bandwidth, simdgroup functions (simd_sum, simd_shuffle), function constants for specialization. Porting via SPIRV-Cross or Metal Shader Converter (DXIL to metallib) for HLSL codebases.

Debugging and profiling: MTL_DEBUG_LAYER=1, MTL_SHADER_VALIDATION=1, Metal shader logging (os_log in MSL with MTLLogState), Xcode GPU frame capture and dependency viewer, programmatic MTLCaptureManager .gputrace captures, Metal Performance HUD (MTL_HUD_ENABLED=1), Instruments Metal System Trace and GPU counters.

Pitfalls: writing shared buffers the GPU is still reading; the wrong sRGB drawable format; HDR without EDR setup (wantsExtendedDynamicRangeContent + rgba16Float + extendedLinearDisplayP3); the 32 KiB threadgroup memory limit; half precision for world positions.

Worked example: port a Vulkan deferred renderer to Metal, keeping the G-buffer on-tile with memoryless attachments and programmable blending. Measure memory bandwidth and frame time with GPU counters before and after on a named Apple GPU.

skills.name: gpu-debugging-profiling
skills.description: GPU-specific shader debugging and profiling across APIs: RenderDoc captures, pixel history and Python replay, Nsight Graphics/Systems/Aftermath, PIX with DRED, the Xcode Metal debugger, Radeon GPU Profiler, Tracy GPU zones, shader printf, debug views, the black-screen checklist, and per-pass timestamp methodology. Load when a frame is wrong, a GPU hangs or crashes, or a pass is too slow; general method lives in debugging-method and performance-optimization.
outline: Tool-selection matrix moved from hub section 11 and gpu-api-map.md sections 4 and 6: RenderDoc (Vulkan/D3D11/D3D12/GL/GLES), Nsight Graphics/Systems/Aftermath (NVIDIA), PIX (D3D12), Xcode Metal debugger + Instruments (Apple), RGP/RGA/Radeon Developer Panel (AMD), Intel GPA, Arm Performance Studio and AGI (mobile), Tracy for CPU+GPU zones, browser tooling for WebGPU.

Capture procedure: renderdoccmd capture or the in-app APIs (StartFrameCapture/EndFrameCapture, PIXBeginCapture, MTLCaptureManager) to grab exactly the failing frame; label every pass (VK_EXT_debug_utils, PIX events, pushDebugGroup) and name every resource.

Wrong-pixel workflow: pixel history -> offending draw -> pipeline state (blend, depth, cull, viewport/scissor) -> shader debugger step-through -> inputs (descriptor contents, buffer viewer format strings) -> mesh viewer before/after transform.

Shader printf and asserts: GL_EXT_debug_printf / HLSL printf through the validation layer's Debug Printf, Metal shader logging, a WGSL debug storage buffer, GPU-assisted validation for out-of-bounds access.
Debug visualization views toggled by define: NaN/Inf in magenta, overdraw, light-count heatmap, mip level, motion vectors, normals, BVH node visits, shadow cascade index.

Black-screen checklist (10 items from hub section 11) and crash triage: device lost/TDR with Aftermath dumps, DRED breadcrumbs and page faults, VK_EXT_device_fault, Metal command-buffer error reports, TDR timeouts on long dispatches.

Profiling method: per-pass GPU timestamps, median of 100+ frames after warm-up, vsync off, fixed resolution. Lock clocks (nvidia-smi --lock-gpu-clocks, D3D12 SetStablePowerState, Nsight lock-to-base). Tell CPU-bound from GPU-bound via timeline gaps (nsys profile -t vulkan,nvtx,osrt).

Reading the bottleneck: Nsight GPU Trace throughput and top limiter, occupancy and register pressure, warp stall reasons; RGP wave occupancy and barrier timing; Xcode per-line shader costs. A limiter -> fix table (bandwidth, ALU, texture, ROP, raster/small triangles, latency).
Regression automation: RenderDoc Python replay (qrenderdoc/renderdoc module) to export per-pass textures from a capture and compare them in CI with FLIP/RMSE thresholds.

Pitfalls: profiling with validation layers on; captures changing timing and hiding races; comparing numbers across driver versions; CPU timers around GPU work; single-run measurements; forgetting to name resources.

Worked example: a 3 ms regression in post-processing. Per-pass timestamps isolate bloom; Nsight shows it texture-bound with 16 full-resolution taps; replace it with a downsampled mip chain. Report medians of 3 runs with GPU, driver and clocks.

skills.name: mesh-processing
skills.description: Polygon mesh processing for rendering and geometry pipelines: validation and repair, vertex normals and MikkTSpace tangents, welding and seams, QEM simplification and LOD chains, isotropic and quad remeshing, UV unwrapping and atlasing, booleans, and GPU-ready optimization and compression with meshoptimizer and gltf-transform. Load when importing, cleaning, decimating, remeshing or exporting meshes.
outline: Stats and validation report before and after every step (from hub section 8): V/E/F, components, boundary loops, non-manifold edges/vertices, degenerate and duplicate faces, winding consistency, genus from V - E + F = 2 - 2g - b. trimesh, PyMeshLab and libigl snippets.

Repair recipes: weld by position within a tolerance only where attributes match (keep UV/normal seams), remove degenerates, orient winding by BFS over faces, fill holes, PyMeshLab filter names for batch scripts.
Normals: angle-weighted face normals, crease splitting at 30-60 degrees, smoothing groups, inverse-transpose under non-uniform scale, renormalization after interpolation and decode.

Tangents: MikkTSpace (glTF requires it when tangents are absent), the w sign for mirrored UVs with bitangent = w*cross(N,T), baker/renderer mismatch symptoms, OpenGL Y+ vs DirectX Y- normal-map conventions.

Simplification: QEM (Garland-Heckbert) Q = sum p p^T with optimal vertex placement, attribute-aware error, border and seam locking. meshopt_simplify / simplifyWithAttributes / simplifySloppy with target error vs index count; LOD chains in ~50% steps selected by screen-space error.

Remeshing: isotropic (Botsch-Kobbelt: split above 4/3 L, collapse below 4/5 L, flip toward valence 6, tangential relaxation, reprojection); quad remeshing with Instant Meshes or QuadriFlow; voxel remesh; CGAL and pmp-library calls.
Parameterization: LSCM/ABF++/SLIM per chart, xatlas packing with mip-safe padding, texel-density checks, lightmap UV rules (no overlaps, gutters).
Booleans: the Manifold library (fast, guaranteed-manifold output), CGAL corefinement or Nef polyhedra for exact arithmetic; inputs must be closed and consistently oriented.

GPU-ready pipeline: meshopt_optimizeVertexCache -> optimizeOverdraw -> optimizeVertexFetch, meshlets (64/124) with bounds and cones, KHR_mesh_quantization, EXT_meshopt_compression or Draco, gltf-transform CLI (weld, simplify, tangents, meshopt, optimize), glTF-Validator.

Pitfalls: welding across UV seams; simplifying non-manifold input; generating tangents before welding; flipped normals after mirroring; dropping skin weights or morph targets during simplification; precision loss on large coordinates.

Worked example: a 3.2M-triangle photogrammetry scan to a real-time glTF. Repair -> isotropic remesh -> QEM to 100k plus LODs -> xatlas UVs -> normal bake -> meshopt + KTX2 -> clean glTF-Validator run, with a stats table at each step.

skills.name: sdf-modeling-raymarching
skills.description: Signed distance fields for modeling and rendering: exact 2D/3D primitives and operators, smooth blends, domain repetition and deformation with Lipschitz bounds, sphere tracing with relaxation, normals, soft shadows and AO, mesh/SDF conversion, sparse SDF storage, and MSDF text rendering. Load for raymarched scenes, procedural modeling, SDF collisions, or SDF fonts and UI.
outline: Primitive and operator sheet expanded from hub section 9: sphere, box, rounded box, capsule, torus, plane; union/intersection/subtraction; polynomial, cubic and exponential smooth-min with blend radius k (quadratic: h = max(k-|a-b|,0)/k, min(a,b) - h^2 k/4). Exact vs bound distances and which operators preserve exactness.

Domain operations: rigid transforms (exact), uniform scale d(p/s)*s, infinite repetition with mod and limited repetition with clamp plus neighbour checks, mirroring, twist/bend (non-Lipschitz: estimate L and divide).

Sphere-tracing loop code: t += d(p)/L; epsilon scaled by pixel footprint t*pixelAngle; 128-256 max steps and a max distance; over-relaxation omega ~1.2-1.6 with fallback (Keinert 2014); bounding volumes and early exit.

Normals and shading: the 4-tap tetrahedron gradient, central differences, analytic gradients; soft shadows res = min(res, k*h/t) and the improved variant; 5-sample SDF AO; fwidth-based edge antialiasing.
Performance: per-object bounds or a BVH over SDF primitives, cone marching or a low-res depth prepass, shader specialization of the SDF tree, per-pixel evaluation budgets, and a step-count heatmap.
SDF to mesh: marching cubes with consistent tables (scikit-image marching_cubes, PyMCubes), dual contouring with a QEF for sharp features, surface nets; grid resolution vs feature size.

Mesh to SDF: sign from generalized winding numbers for non-watertight input (Jacobson 2013), unsigned distance via BVH closest-point queries, fast sweeping, OpenVDB meshToVolume and NanoVDB on GPU, 3D textures and brick maps.
2D SDFs for UI and text: msdfgen/msdf-atlas-gen MSDF fonts, median(r,g,b) reconstruction, screenPxRange scaling, outlines, shadows and glows derived from distance.
Validation: numerically check the Lipschitz bound (sample |grad d| <= 1 over random points) and compare against brute-force mesh distance on a test grid.

Pitfalls: overstepping from non-Lipschitz operations (holes, banding); epsilon too small (stalls) or too large (bloat); precision far from the origin; normals across smooth-min seams; MSDF corner artifacts from a wrong pxRange.
Worked example: a twisted, repeated column scene shows holes. Estimate L by sampling (~2.3), divide the step, add the relaxation fallback, and report step heatmaps and frame time before and after.

skills.name: color-pipeline-tonemapping
skills.description: Scene-referred color management for renderers and image tools: sRGB/linear decode and encode, primaries and white points (Rec.709, P3, Rec.2020, ACEScg), OCIO configs, exposure and auto-exposure, tonemappers (AgX, ACES 2.0, Khronos PBR Neutral, Reinhard), HDR output (PQ, scRGB, EDR), banding, alpha and gamut mapping. Load when images look washed out, too dark, hue-shifted or banded, or wrong on HDR displays.
outline: Pipeline order and per-buffer convention table (moved from hub section 7 and color-pipeline.md): decode -> linear working space -> exposure -> display transform -> encode. Which inputs are _SRGB (baseColor, emissive, UI) vs UNORM (normal, roughness, metal, AO, masks, LUTs).

Spaces and matrices: a primaries/white/transfer table, sRGB<->XYZ and Rec.709->Rec.2020 matrices, Bradford adaptation, ACEScg (AP1) for wide gamut. Prefer OpenColorIO 2.4+ configs (ACES studio config, Blender AgX) and the Python colour-science package over hand-typed matrices.
Transfer functions with exact constants: sRGB piecewise encode/decode, BT.1886, PQ ST 2084 (m1, m2, c1-c3), HLG. GPU _SRGB formats decode on sample and encode on write.

Exposure: EV100 from camera settings (log2(N^2/t) - log2(S/100)) or the scene (log2(L_avg*S/K), K=12.5), L_max = 1.2*2^EV100. Auto-exposure from a 64-256 bin log-luminance histogram averaged over the 50th-95th percentile, with asymmetric adaptation speeds.

Display transforms with code: Reinhard and extended Reinhard, the Narkowicz ACES fit, ACES 2.0 output transforms via OCIO, AgX (Blender 4.x, three.js AgXToneMapping), Khronos PBR Neutral. Per-channel hue skews (the 'notorious six') vs luminance-preserving operators.

HDR output: a paper-white slider (203 nits per BT.2408), querying display peak (DXGI output desc, EDR headroom, WebGPU toneMapping extended), PQ Rec.2020 HDR10 vs scRGB FP16, UI composited at paper white and never tonemapped.
Quantization: RGBA16F vs R11G11B10F trade-offs; triangular-pdf dither of +/-1 LSB before 8/10-bit output; never store 8-bit linear color.
Alpha and blending: premultiplied alpha end to end, blending in linear space, sRGB mip generation in linear, diagnosing dark fringes.
Gamut mapping: OKLCh chroma reduction at constant lightness and hue, or ACES/OCIO gamut compression, instead of per-channel clipping of negative components.

Checks: 0.18 linear should encode to ~0.46 (about 118/255); push a gray ramp and a ColorChecker through the pipeline and compare against ocioconvert; with an identity tonemap, sunlit white diffuse should be about 2.9e4 cd/m^2 in physical units.
Pitfalls: double encode or decode; albedo loaded as linear; normal maps loaded as sRGB; tonemapping applied twice (post plus UI); 8-bit HDR targets; tonemapping the UI; blending in gamma space.

Worked example: a glTF viewer renders too dark and oversaturated because the loader marked every map sRGB and the swapchain is UNORM with no encode. Fix per-map color spaces, switch to an _SRGB swapchain and add PBR Neutral; verify middle gray and ColorChecker deltaE2000 against a reference viewer.

skills.name: gpu-compute-patterns
skills.description: Data-parallel GPU compute building blocks across CUDA, HLSL, GLSL/Vulkan, Metal and WGSL: thread-hierarchy mapping, reductions, prefix scans (reduce-then-scan vs decoupled look-back), radix sort, stream compaction, histograms, tiled shared memory, subgroup/wave intrinsics, atomics, indirect dispatch, and occupancy/coalescing rules. Load when writing or optimizing a compute kernel or porting one between APIs.
outline: Terminology map: thread/invocation/lane; warp/wave/subgroup/simdgroup widths (32 NVIDIA, 32/64 AMD, 32 Apple, 8-32 Intel and mobile, variable in WebGPU); block/workgroup/threadgroup; shared/groupshared/threadgroup/var<workgroup>; barrier and memory-scope names per API.

Launch sizing: workgroups of 64-256, dispatch = ceil(n/size) with a bounds check, grid-stride loops, occupancy limited by registers and shared memory, 65535 groups per dimension, splitting long dispatches to stay under the TDR timeout.

Memory rules: coalesced access (consecutive lanes hit consecutive addresses), AoS vs SoA, shared-memory bank conflicts (32 banks x 4 bytes, pad tiles to [32][33]), cache vs texture paths, uniform/constant buffers for broadcast data.

Reduction: per-lane accumulation -> subgroup reduce (WaveActiveSum, subgroupAdd, simd_sum, __reduce_add_sync) -> shared memory -> one atomic or a second pass; notes on float non-determinism and Kahan or pairwise sums.

Prefix scan: work-efficient Blelloch in shared memory; subgroup inclusive scans; single-pass decoupled look-back (Merrill-Garland 2016) only where forward progress is guaranteed (not Apple, mobile or WebGPU); reduce-then-scan as the portable default.

Radix sort: 8-bit digits in 4 passes for 32-bit keys, a global histogram plus Onesweep (Adinets-Merrill 2022), or FidelityFX Parallel Sort / CUB DeviceRadixSort; key-value pairs and the float-key bit flip (sign-bit tricks).
Stream compaction and append: subgroup ballot/popcount with one atomic per subgroup, or scan + scatter; indirect dispatch/draw arguments written on the GPU; append-order caveats.
Histograms and atomics: privatized shared-memory histograms merged at the end, contention costs, availability of 64-bit and float atomics per API, atomic memory-ordering semantics.
Tiling patterns: tiled matrix multiply and convolution with shared-memory halos, separable filters, ping-pong buffers, cooperative loads of neighbour data.
Libraries and port table: CUB/Thrust (CUDA 12/13), rocPRIM/hipCUB, FidelityFX SDK, Metal Performance Shaders, Kokkos/SYCL, hand-written kernels for wgpu/WebGPU; mapping each primitive across APIs.

Verification and measurement: a CPU reference with edge-case sizes (0, 1, non-multiples of the workgroup, 2^24+1) and adversarial data; effective GB/s vs peak bandwidth; Nsight Compute, RGP and Xcode counters.
Worked example: a portable 32-bit key radix sort in WGSL and HLSL using reduce-then-scan per digit on 1M keys. Validate against std::sort and report Mkeys/s on two named GPUs.

skills.name: denoising-taa-upscaling
skills.description: Reconstructing clean frames from noisy or aliased input: OIDN and OptiX offline denoising, SVGF and NRD real-time denoisers, MSAA/FXAA/SMAA, TAA jitter and history rejection, and DLSS/FSR/XeSS/MetalFX integration through motion vectors, jitter, exposure and reactive masks. Load when renders are noisy, edges crawl, TAA ghosts or blurs, or a denoiser or upscaler is being integrated.
outline: Decision table: offline final frames (OIDN 2.x, OptiX 9 AOV/temporal) vs interactive viewport vs real-time 1 spp (SVGF/A-SVGF, NRD ReBLUR/ReLAX/SIGMA, vendor ML); AA choice (MSAA, FXAA/SMAA, TAA, upscalers) by pipeline (forward, deferred, visibility buffer); DLSS Ray Reconstruction and FSR Redstone replace denoiser plus upscaler.

Input contract: linear HDR pre-tonemap colour, first-hit albedo, normals in the expected space, roughness, viewZ/depth with reversed-Z flag, motion vectors with sign and units, hit distance, exposure, reactive and transparency masks, jitter offsets.
OIDN: device + filter 'RT' with color/albedo/normal, hdr flag, quality HIGH/BALANCED/FAST, cleanAux for noisy guides; CLI oidnDenoise --hdr color.pfm --alb albedo.pfm --nrm normal.pfm -o out.pfm.
Demodulation: divide irradiance by albedo (+eps) before filtering and remodulate after; separate diffuse, specular and shadow signals; emissive surfaces on their own path.

SVGF: reprojected accumulation with depth/normal disocclusion tests and alpha ~0.2, temporal-moment variance, 5 a-trous passes with edge-stopping (sigma_z = 1, sigma_n = 128, sigma_l = 4), A-SVGF gradient history reset; NRD packing helpers, matrices, jitter and history reset on cuts.
MSAA with Karis 1/(1+luma) resolve and alpha-to-coverage; FXAA 3.11 after tonemapping; SMAA 1x/T2x stages and presets.

TAA: Halton(2,3) jitter with 8-16 phases added to the projection, unjittered matrices for motion vectors, mip bias; resolve with dilated motion vectors, Catmull-Rom history, YCoCg variance clipping (gamma ~1), alpha 0.05-0.1, luma weighting, disocclusion and camera-cut resets.

Motion vectors for everything: per-object previous transforms, skinned meshes with previous joint palettes, vertex animation, particles and UV scrolling via reactive masks, camera-only vectors for the background.

Upscaler integration (DLSS 4 via Streamline, FSR 3.1/4, XeSS 2, MetalFX, TSR): render-resolution presets, LOD bias ~log2(render/display) confirmed per SDK, UI and late post after the upscale, CAS/RCAS sharpening without double sharpening.

Evaluation: FLIP and relMSE against a converged reference at 1/4/16 spp, a flicker metric from frame differences on a static camera, ghosting tests with moving lights and objects, crops saved to out_dir.

Pitfalls: tonemapped or sRGB input, NaN/Inf poisoning history, fireflies not clamped before accumulation, wrong motion-vector sign or units, jitter applied twice, specular denoised with diffuse settings, UI drawn before TAA, history kept across lighting changes.

Worked example: 1-spp RT GI that flickers and smears plus TAA ghost trails behind a rotating fan; fixes are demodulation, hit distance, A-SVGF reset, per-object motion vectors and variance clipping; flicker metric and FLIP before/after.

skills.name: algorithm-design-paradigms
skills.description: Algorithm design from a problem statement: formalise, recognise the classic problem in disguise, pick a paradigm (greedy, divide and conquer, search, solver, streaming, online) and meet its proof obligation, then verify with a brute-force oracle and differential tests. Load when designing an algorithm or judging whether a proposed approach is correct.
outline: Formalisation template: input, output, objective, constraints, sizes n/m and value ranges, machine model (word RAM, comparison, external memory B/M, work-span). Size-to-budget table at ~10^8 simple ops/s per core: n<=10 -> n!, <=20 -> 2^n, <=500 -> n^3, <=5000 -> n^2, <=10^6 -> n log n, <=10^8 -> n.

Recognition catalogue mapping problem signals to classics: interval scheduling/partitioning, LIS, edit distance, knapsack, bipartite matching, min-cut/closure, 2-SAT, shortest paths, topological order, union-find connectivity, sweep line, two pointers/sliding window, monotone stack, binary search on the answer / parametric search.

Paradigm decision table with each paradigm's proof obligation, kept from cs-foundations §1: DP state/recurrence, greedy exchange argument, D&C recurrence, graph modelling, backtracking pruning soundness, solver encodings, randomisation bounds, sketches eps/delta, online competitive ratio, FPT, approximation ratio, preprocessing vs query cost.

Greedy proofs: exchange-argument template (take an OPT that agrees on the longest prefix, swap, show it is no worse), the stays-ahead argument, and the matroid test (hereditary + exchange property means greedy is optimal for max-weight independent set). Always run a brute-force counterexample search for n<=8 before writing the proof.

Divide and conquer and search: combine-step cost, base-case cutoffs for constants, classics (closest pair, inversion counting, median of medians, FFT multiplication); backtracking with pruning, branch-and-bound bound validity, meet-in-the-middle 2^(n/2), IDA*, A* with admissible/consistent heuristics.

Hand-off to solvers (2026): OR-Tools CP-SAT, HiGHS and Gurobi for MILP, CaDiCaL/Kissat for SAT, Z3/cvc5 for SMT, MiniZinc for modelling. Encoding tips: symmetry breaking, tight big-M, redundant constraints. Always report the time limit, the optimality gap and whether the result is proven optimal.

Workhorse techniques with invariants written out: prefix sums and difference arrays, coordinate compression, event-sorted sweep line, sliding window with a monotone deque, and binary search on a monotone predicate using the lo/hi invariant template that avoids off-by-one errors.

Verification loop: an exhaustive brute-force oracle for n<=8, seeded random differential testing (10^4-10^6 cases), shrinking the first counterexample with Hypothesis or proptest, and an empirical scaling check (log-log slope over >=5 sizes). Generic harness mechanics are delegated to testing-strategy.

Pitfalls: greedy without a proof; integer overflow (use 64-bit or checked arithmetic); recursion depth (Python's limit is 1000, so go iterative or use an explicit stack); comparators that are not strict weak orderings; floating-point geometry predicates (use exact integer orientation tests or a stated epsilon policy).

Worked example: weighted interval scheduling. Show that greedy by earliest finish fails on a 3-interval weighted counterexample, give the DP over end-sorted intervals with binary-searched predecessor p(j), OPT(j)=max(OPT(j-1), w_j+OPT(p(j))) in O(n log n), reconstruct by re-walking, and differentially test against 2^n subset enumeration for n<=12.

skills.name: dynamic-programming-patterns
skills.description: Dynamic programming design and optimisation: state, recurrence, evaluation order, base cases and reconstruction; the classic families (knapsack, LIS, alignment, interval, tree, bitmask, digit, DAG, profile DP); speedups (monotone queue, convex hull trick/Li Chao, divide-and-conquer and Knuth optimisation, SOS, Aliens trick, matrix power); and memory reduction. Load when a problem has overlapping subproblems or an existing DP is too slow or too large.
outline: Five-step recipe: (1) define the state in words ('dp[i][j] = min cost using the first i items with j units used'); (2) write the transition; (3) choose an evaluation order that is a topological order of the state DAG; (4) set base cases and impossible states (-inf/+inf, never 0) and extract the answer; (5) cost = #states x transition cost. Reconstruct with parent pointers or by re-walking the table.

Top-down vs bottom-up: use memoisation (functools.cache, a HashMap) when reachable states are sparse and a table when they are dense. Covers Python recursion limits, memo keys that must capture all state, lru_cache on unhashable or mutable arguments, and cycles in the state graph (which need Bellman-Ford or a fixpoint, not DP).

Family catalogue with state and complexity: 0/1 knapsack O(nW) (1-D table, capacity loop downward) vs unbounded (loop upward); subset-sum bitset bits |= bits<<a in O(nT/w); LIS by patience/tails in O(n log n); LCS and edit distance O(nm); interval/matrix-chain O(n^3); tree DP with rerooting for all roots in O(n); bitmask TSP O(2^n n^2) for n<=20-23; digit DP state (pos, tight, started, aux); longest path in a DAG; broken-profile tiling; expected-value DP.

Transition speedups and when each applies: monotone deque for sliding-window min/max transitions (O(n)); convex hull trick / Li Chao tree for dp[i]=min_j(m_j*x_i+b_j) (O(n log n)); divide-and-conquer optimisation when opt(i,j) is monotone (O(kn log n)); Knuth optimisation under the quadrangle inequality (O(n^3) -> O(n^2)); SOS DP (O(n 2^n)); matrix exponentiation for linear recurrences (O(k^3 log n)).
Dimension removal: the Aliens trick (WQS / Lagrangian binary search on a penalty lambda) when the answer is convex in the count k, including how to handle ties at the breakpoint.
Memory reduction: rolling two rows, the 1-D in-place direction rule, Hirschberg divide and conquer for alignment reconstruction in O(min(n,m)) space, and checkpoint/recompute for long chains.

Correctness argument: optimal substructure by cut-and-paste, induction over the evaluation order, and differential testing of the DP against brute-force enumeration on small inputs. State plainly that O(nW) is pseudo-polynomial (exponential in input bits) and cross-link to np-hardness-reductions.

Numerics and engineering: counting modulo a prime or with u128/BigInt; probability DP in log space with logsumexp; vectorising row updates with NumPy; bitset tricks (Python int, std::bitset, Rust bitvec); cache-friendly loop order (inner loop over the contiguous dimension).

Pitfalls: a state that is missing a dimension (e.g. the last item used or the current tightness), wrong loop direction for 0/1 vs unbounded knapsack, initialising impossible states to 0, overlapping subproblems silently recomputed because of an un-memoised helper, off-by-one in the 1-indexed vs 0-indexed table.

Worked example: split an array into k contiguous segments minimising the sum of (segment sum)^2. Start from the naive O(kn^2) DP, prove opt monotonicity from the quadrangle inequality, apply divide-and-conquer optimisation for O(kn log n), then the Aliens trick for O(n log n log C). Each version is differentially tested against brute force for n<=10 and timed at n=2^12..2^16.

skills.name: graph-algorithms
skills.description: Graph modelling and algorithm choice: representation, traversal and ordering (BFS, DFS, topological sort, SCC, bridges, 2-SAT), shortest paths (0-1 BFS, Dijkstra, Bellman-Ford, Johnson, Floyd-Warshall, A*), spanning trees, max-flow/min-cut modelling, matchings and assignment. Includes library calls (NetworkX, rustworkx, igraph, graph-tool, NetworKit, scipy.csgraph, OR-Tools, petgraph, Boost.Graph) and certificate checks. Load for dependency, routing, reachability, assignment or capacity problems.
outline: Modelling step: decide what a vertex and an edge are; directed or not; weight sign and range; multi-edges; implicit graphs (grids, state spaces) vs materialised ones. Choose the representation from V/E: CSR for large static graphs, a bitset adjacency matrix for dense graphs up to about 10^4 vertices, an edge list for Kruskal/streaming.

Shortest-path decision table: unweighted -> BFS O(V+E); 0/1 weights -> 0-1 BFS with a deque; non-negative -> Dijkstra with a binary heap and lazy deletion O((V+E) log V); negative edges -> Bellman-Ford O(VE) with negative-cycle detection (SPFA has the same worst case); DAG -> topological relaxation; all pairs dense -> Floyd-Warshall O(V^3); sparse with negatives -> Johnson reweighting; single pair -> A* or bidirectional search; road networks -> contraction hierarchies (OSRM, RoutingKit).

Structure algorithms with use cases: Kahn topological sort with cycle report, Tarjan/Kosaraju SCC plus the condensation DAG, 2-SAT via the implication graph, bridges and articulation points via low-link, Hierholzer Euler paths, bipartiteness by BFS 2-colouring, LCA by binary lifting or Euler tour plus sparse table.
MST: Kruskal with union-find, Prim with a heap, Boruvka for parallel or external settings; the cut and cycle properties as proof tools; minimum bottleneck paths taken from the MST.

Flow modelling cookbook: Dinic (O(V^2 E); O(E sqrt V) on unit networks) vs push-relabel (highest-label plus gap heuristic for dense graphs). Min-cut extraction from residual reachability. Tricks: vertex capacities by node splitting, a super source/sink, lower bounds via demands, project selection / max-weight closure as min-cut, edge-disjoint paths. Min-cost flow by successive shortest paths with potentials, or network simplex (OR-Tools SimpleMinCostFlow, LEMON).

Matching and assignment: Hopcroft-Karp O(E sqrt V); Konig's theorem (min vertex cover = max matching in bipartite graphs) with cover extraction; Hungarian / Jonker-Volgenant via scipy.optimize.linear_sum_assignment for weighted assignment; Edmonds blossom for general graphs (networkx.max_weight_matching); Gale-Shapley stable matching.

2026 library cheat sheet with scale limits: NetworkX (pure Python, fine up to ~10^5 edges, also the reference oracle), rustworkx, igraph, graph-tool and NetworKit (C/C++ cores, 10^7-10^9 edges), scipy.sparse.csgraph (shortest_path, maximum_flow, min_weight_full_bipartite_matching), OR-Tools, petgraph, Boost.Graph, cuGraph on GPU.

Certificate checks instead of trusting output: shortest-path potentials satisfy d[v] <= d[u]+w(u,v) with equality on tree edges; max-flow value = cut capacity; matching size = Konig cover size; flow conservation at every vertex; topological order respects every edge.

Pitfalls: Dijkstra with negative edges silently returns wrong answers; INF + w overflow (use INF = 2^62 and check before adding); recursive DFS overflows at 10^6 vertices (use an explicit stack); visited-on-push vs visited-on-pop errors; undirected edges stored once; parallel and anti-parallel edges in flow networks; floating-point capacities without an epsilon.

Worked example: assign reviewers to papers with per-reviewer load limits, k reviews per paper and conflicts of interest. Model as a b-matching via max-flow with a super source and sink, extend to min-cost flow for preference costs, verify conservation and optimality against OR-Tools on seeded random instances, and report a min-cut as the certificate when demand cannot be met.

skills.name: string-algorithms
skills.description: String and sequence algorithms with production implementations: single- and multi-pattern exact search (prefix function/KMP, Z, Horspool, two-way, Aho-Corasick), rolling hashes with collision math, suffix arrays with LCP, suffix automata, BWT/FM-index, approximate matching (banded and bit-parallel edit distance, BK-trees, n-gram indexes), and Unicode correctness. Load when searching, indexing, deduplicating or comparing text, logs or sequences.
outline: Decision table from task to algorithm, complexity and library: memchr/memmem crate or glibc memmem (two-way); Python str.find (two-way for long needles since 3.10); the aho-corasick crate (Teddy SIMD) and pyahocorasick; ripgrep and Hyperscan/Vectorscan for many patterns; libsais/pydivsufsort; rapidfuzz, edlib and parasail for approximate and alignment work.

Prefix function and Z-function: definitions, O(n+m) construction code, and uses: occurrence counting via pattern + sentinel + text, the period of a string (n - pi[n-1] when it divides n), the border tree, and string compression checks.

Rolling hash done safely: a polynomial hash mod 2^61-1 with a random base, collision probability <= (n-1)/p per comparison, why mod 2^64 breaks on Thue-Morse strings, double hashing, and always verifying candidate matches. Uses: O(1) substring equality, and longest repeated substring by binary search plus a hash set.

Aho-Corasick: trie, BFS failure links and output (dictionary) links; O(n + sum m + z); overlapping vs leftmost-first vs leftmost-longest semantics (configurable in the Rust crate); memory for large dictionaries (double-array tries, DFA vs NFA mode).

Suffix array toolkit: SA-IS/libsais O(n) vs a simple O(n log n) prefix-doubling implementation, Kasai LCP O(n), pattern search O(m log n) (O(m + log n) with LCP), distinct substrings = n(n+1)/2 - sum LCP, longest repeated substring = max LCP, LCS of two strings via a sentinel concatenation. The suffix automaton alternative has <= 2n-1 states.

BWT/FM-index: backward search, occ/rank structures and sampling rate trade-offs, compressed full-text indexes (sdsl-lite, r-index), and bioinformatics aligners (BWA-MEM2, bowtie2, minimap2 for long reads) as reference implementations.

Approximate matching: Levenshtein O(nm), banded O(nk) for threshold k, Myers/Hyyro bit-parallel O(n ceil(m/w)), Damerau vs OSA distinction, Jaro-Winkler for names, trigram indexes (PostgreSQL pg_trgm), BK-trees, SymSpell deletion dictionaries. The SETH lower bound means no strongly subquadratic exact edit distance.

Unicode correctness: bytes vs code points vs grapheme clusters (UAX #29: unicode-segmentation, ICU, Python regex \X); NFC/NFKC normalisation before comparing (UAX #15); casefold() not lower() (Turkish dotted/dotless i, German sharp s); UTF-16 surrogate lengths in Java and JS; ICU collation for sorting; confusables/skeletons (UTS #39) for identifier spoofing.

Pitfalls: quadratic s += t in loops (use a builder or join); hidden substring copies; naive find with O(nm) worst case on adversarial input; treating a hash match as equality; a sentinel that collides with the alphabet; mixing byte and character offsets across APIs.

Worked example: find the longest substring that appears in at least k of N log files. Build a generalised suffix array with distinct sentinels, compute LCP, slide a window over SA positions covering k distinct sources using a monotone deque for the window min LCP (O(total length)), cross-check against brute force on small corpora, and note MinHash/LSH (randomized-algorithms-sketches) for fuzzy near-duplicates.

skills.name: data-structure-selection
skills.description: Choosing data structures from the operation mix: dictionaries and ordered maps, priority queues, sequences, range-query structures, spatial and vector indexes, persistent structures and graph representations, with asymptotic costs, cache and allocation constants, concrete per-language library picks (2026), adversarial-key defences and a benchmark-to-confirm step. Load when picking, reviewing or replacing a container, index or in-memory structure.
outline: Selection procedure: list operations with frequencies, sizes and key distributions; derive the required complexities; shortlist candidates; compare constants (cache misses ~100 ns each, allocations, pointer chasing); check library availability; confirm with a microbenchmark on realistic data. State which two of read, update and memory overhead you optimise (RUM conjecture).

Dictionary/set table kept from the reference: chaining vs open addressing (linear, Robin Hood, Swiss) with load-factor limits, cuckoo, RB/AVL, in-memory B-tree, skip list, treap/splay, radix/ART, sorted array with Eytzinger layout, vEB/y-fast for integer universes.

Per-language picks: Rust (HashMap = hashbrown SwissTable with SipHash-1-3; foldhash/ahash for trusted keys; BTreeMap; indexmap), C++ (avoid node-based std::unordered_map on hot paths; absl::flat_hash_map / boost::unordered_flat_map; C++23 std::flat_map), Java (HashMap treeifies buckets at 8; fastutil/Eclipse Collections primitive maps), Go (map is a Swiss table since 1.24; google/btree, tidwall/btree), Python (dict, collections.deque, heapq, bisect, sortedcontainers), Haskell (Data.Map, IntMap, HashMap HAMT), Julia (Dict, DataStructures.jl).

Priority queue table and advice: a binary or 4-ary heap with lazy deletion beats Fibonacci heaps for Dijkstra in practice; an indexed heap when real decrease-key is needed; radix heaps for monotone integer keys; pairing heaps when melds dominate.

Sequences: dynamic-array growth factor 1.5-2 and amortised push, ring-buffer deques, rope / piece table / gap buffer for editors, RRB vectors / finger trees / HAMTs for persistence, order-statistic trees for k-th element and rank.

Range-query table: Fenwick for invertible operations, segment tree with lazy propagation for any monoid, sparse table O(1) static RMQ, LCA via Euler tour, interval trees, merge-sort or wavelet tree for k-th smallest in a range, Mo's algorithm and sqrt decomposition for offline queries, 2-D prefix sums.

Spatial and vector: k-d tree (effective up to ~10-20 dimensions), R*-tree / PostGIS GiST for rectangles, quadtrees, BVH, geohash/S2/H3 cells, and HNSW or IVF-PQ ANN indexes (hnswlib, FAISS, pgvector, usearch) for embeddings, with the recall/latency/memory trade-off stated.

Graph representations from the reference (CSR, bitset matrix, edge list, union-find, link-cut / Euler-tour trees), plus persistent structures via path copying at O(log n) per version, and when immutability pays (snapshots, undo, lock-free readers).
Adversarial keys: keyed hashes (SipHash) or randomised seeds for untrusted input; HashDoS; Java treeification as a mitigation; never expose hash iteration order in APIs.

Pitfalls: Python list.pop(0) and x in list are O(n); Java LinkedList almost never wins; iterator invalidation on rehash or vector growth; mutable keys inside hash sets; small-n cases where a linear scan of a flat array beats any tree (measure below ~32-64 elements); SmallVec/InlinedVector for tiny collections.

Worked example: a leaderboard with 10^6 players, 50k score updates/s, top-100 and rank-of-player queries. Compare an order-statistic tree / skip list (Redis sorted set = skip list + hash) with a Fenwick tree over bounded integer score buckets: costs, memory, and a benchmark plan with a Zipf update distribution and a decision rule.

skills.name: np-hardness-reductions
skills.description: Hardness and lower bounds done right: the complexity class map, polynomial-time reduction procedure (direction, both implications, size and number magnitude), a source-problem catalogue and gadget checklist, strong vs weak NP-hardness, the escape table (pseudo-polynomial, FPT, special structure, approximation, solvers), inapproximability and W-hardness, fine-grained conjectures, model-specific lower bounds, and undecidability via Rice. Load for 'is this NP-hard', 'can we do better' or any impossibility claim.
outline: Class map kept from the reference: P, NP, coNP, NP intersect coNP, #P, PSPACE, EXPTIME, BPP/RP/ZPP, BQP, L/NL, with complete problems, the known inclusions and separations, and the open questions.

Five-step reduction procedure kept from §4: choose a source Y; map Y <=_p X (known-hard to new problem); prove both implications; check output size and the magnitude of numbers; show membership in NP for completeness. Also covers Karp vs Cook reductions and approximation-preserving reductions (L-reductions, gap-preserving).

Source catalogue kept and extended: 3-SAT variants (planar, monotone rectilinear, bounded occurrence), NAE-3SAT and 1-in-3-SAT, vertex cover / independent set / clique (cubic, planar), 3-colouring, Hamiltonian cycle (cubic planar, grid graphs for puzzles), 3-dimensional matching, Partition vs 3-Partition, X3C, max-cut, Steiner tree, dominating set.

Gadget checklist: a variable gadget forces a binary choice; a clause gadget is satisfiable iff one literal is true; degree and planarity preserved when needed. Extract an assignment from ANY target solution, including unintended ones, and count the polynomial size and the unary vs binary number encoding.

Escape table kept from §4 (pseudo-polynomial DP, FPT parameter, special structure, approximation, solver plus heuristics, fast exponential such as meet-in-the-middle and inclusion-exclusion), with a rule to check real instance sizes and structure before declaring a problem intractable.

Approximation and hardness table kept from the reference (vertex cover 2 / 2-eps under UGC, set cover ln n, max-3SAT 7/8, max-cut 0.878, metric TSP ~1.5, Euclidean TSP PTAS, bin packing, knapsack FPTAS, clique n^(1-eps), k-center 2), plus FPT vs W[1]/W[2], kernelisation, ETH and SETH.

Fine-grained conjectures table (SETH -> OV/edit distance/LCS/diameter; 3SUM; APSP; OMv; combinatorial BMM), used to justify that 'quadratic is likely optimal'. Always label such statements as conditional.

Lower-bound techniques with their models: decision tree / information theory (log2 n! comparisons), adversary arguments (max+min in ceil(3n/2)-2), reductions from element distinctness, communication complexity for streaming, and cell-probe. A bound holds only in its model (radix sort and hashing escape it).

Undecidability: Rice's theorem and halting reductions; say whether a static analyser is sound-but-incomplete or complete-but-unsound; semi-decidability and what is still achievable (bounded checking, abstraction).

Mechanical check of a reduction: on all small source instances (e.g. Partition with n<=8 and values <=10), solve source and image by brute force or a SAT encoding (PySAT) and assert the answers match. Also check that the map runs in polynomial time and produces values of bounded magnitude.

Pitfalls: reducing in the wrong direction; calling pseudo-polynomial polynomial; hardness of a general problem used to dismiss small or structured real instances; hardness of a special case confused with hardness of yours; promising an approximation ratio below a known inapproximability bound.

Worked example kept from §12: 2-machine makespan from Partition, with both directions proved and the linear-time map. It is only weakly NP-hard (O(nS) DP); 3-Partition gives strong hardness for m as input; LPT achieves 4/3 - 1/(3m); the practical recommendation is DP when S is small.

skills.name: amortized-recurrence-analysis
skills.description: Proving running-time bounds: cost models and measures (worst, expected, amortised, average, w.h.p.), recurrences (master theorem with its gaps, Akra-Bazzi, recursion trees, substitution, characteristic roots), amortised analysis by aggregate, accounting and potential methods with standard potentials, de-amortisation for latency, competitive analysis, work-span bounds, and empirical scaling checks. Load when deriving, proving or disputing a complexity bound.
outline: Declare the model and measure first (kept from §2): word RAM with w = Theta(log n), comparison, external memory (B, M), or work-span; worst, expected (algorithm randomness), average (with the stated distribution), amortised, or w.h.p. Hidden costs: hashing is O(1) only in expectation, big integers are not O(1), string comparison is O(length), recursion depth.

Master theorem table kept from §2, plus where it fails: f(n) = n/log n with a = b = 2 gives Theta(n log log n) and is outside the three cases; non-polynomial gaps; floors and ceilings. The Akra-Bazzi formula with a worked unequal split T(n/3)+T(2n/3)+n.

Other recurrence methods: recursion trees (sum per level, identify the dominant level), substitution with a strengthened hypothesis (T(n) <= cn - d), characteristic roots for linear recurrences, a generating-function shortcut, and the recurrences cheat sheet table kept from the reference (median of medians, T(sqrt n), n log^2 n cases).
Aggregate method with examples: binary counter (<= 2n bit flips over n increments), monotone stack and deque (each element pushed and popped once), BFS edge scanning, KMP failure-pointer walk.

Accounting method: dynamic-array doubling with credit 3 per push; shrink at 1/4 occupancy (not 1/2) to avoid thrashing; credit invariants written as an explicit statement that is checked at each operation.

Potential method with a standard-potential table: dynamic array Phi = 2*size - capacity; binary counter Phi = number of ones; two-stack queue Phi = 2*|inbox|; splay tree Phi = sum of log subtree sizes (access lemma -> O(log n)); union-find with rank and path compression O(alpha(n)); Fibonacci heap Phi = trees + 2*marked. Requirements: Phi >= 0 and Phi_0 = 0.

Amortised vs latency: amortised bounds do not bound per-request p99 (rehash spikes, GC, compaction). De-amortisation techniques: incremental rehash as in Redis, real-time queues (Hood-Melville), and laziness plus memoisation for persistent structures (Okasaki's banker's method), since persistence breaks naive amortisation.

Expected bounds: linearity of expectation with indicator variables (randomised quicksort 2n ln n ~ 1.39 n log2 n comparisons), plus a pointer to randomized-algorithms-sketches for Chernoff-style w.h.p. bounds.

Online and parallel bounds: competitive analysis (ski rental 2 deterministic and e/(e-1) randomised, LRU k-competitive paging, move-to-front 2-competitive); work-span with Brent's bound T_p <= W/p + D; the parallel prefix-sum example.

Empirical check: instrument operation counters rather than wall time to remove cache effects, run n = 2^k for >= 5 sizes across >= 2 decades, fit the log-log slope with numpy.polyfit, and separate n log n from n^1.1 by plotting T/(n log n). Statistics are delegated to performance-optimization.

Pitfalls: an amortised bound quoted for an SLO; an average-case result over a uniform distribution presented as worst case; O() hiding 10^3 constants; adversarial inputs defeating expected bounds when the seed is fixed or exposed.

Worked example: prove a two-stack queue is O(1) amortised with Phi = 2*|inbox| (push 3, pop 1, transfer amortised 1), show the O(n) worst-case spike, de-amortise to a real-time queue when p99 matters, and verify with op counters over 10^6 random operation sequences.

skills.name: randomized-algorithms-sketches
skills.description: Randomised algorithms and probabilistic data structures: Las Vegas vs Monte Carlo and amplification, tail bounds (Markov, Chebyshev, Chernoff, Hoeffding, union, birthday), hash families, sampling, sketches (Bloom/cuckoo/binary fuse filters, count-min, HyperLogLog, KLL/t-digest, MinHash/LSH, JL projections) with sizing formulas and libraries, classic randomised algorithms, and reproducible RNG engineering. Load when designing with randomness, sizing a sketch, or bounding a failure probability.
outline: Error types and amplification: Las Vegas vs Monte Carlo, one-sided vs two-sided error; k independent repeats drive one-sided error to 2^-k; majority vote with k = O(log 1/delta) for two-sided error via Chernoff; converting Las Vegas to Monte Carlo with a Markov-bounded timeout.

Tail-bound cheat sheet with formulas and when each applies: Markov; Chebyshev; multiplicative Chernoff P(X >= (1+d)mu) <= exp(-d^2 mu/3) for 0 < d <= 1 and P(X <= (1-d)mu) <= exp(-d^2 mu/2); Hoeffding 2exp(-2nt^2/(b-a)^2); the union bound; the birthday bound n^2/(2m); coupon collector n H_n (full catalogue and conditions in probability-distributions-limits).

Hashing for algorithms: universal ((ax+b) mod p) mod m and multiply-shift; pairwise independence suffices for count-min; linear probing needs 5-independence or tabulation hashing; fast practical hashes (xxh3, wyhash/rapidhash) vs SipHash for untrusted keys; Kirsch-Mitzenmacher double hashing g_i = h1 + i*h2 for k Bloom hashes.

Sampling: reservoir Algorithm R and skip-based Algorithm L; weighted A-Res (key u^(1/w)); priority and stratified sampling; Fisher-Yates shuffle (sorting with a random comparator is biased); sampling without replacement from huge ranges (Floyd's algorithm).

Membership filters with formulas: Bloom m = -n ln p/(ln 2)^2 and k = (m/n) ln 2 (1% -> 9.6 bits/key, 0.1% -> 14.4); blocked Bloom (one cache line per query); counting Bloom; cuckoo and quotient filters (deletes); binary fuse / XOR (static, ~1.13 log2(1/p) bits/key). The FPR explodes when n exceeds the design capacity.

Counting and quantiles: HyperLogLog/HLL++ standard error 1.04/sqrt(m) (2^14 registers ~12 KB -> 0.81%), sparse mode, merging, small-range bias; count-min w = ceil(e/eps), d = ceil(ln 1/delta); count sketch; Misra-Gries / Space-Saving top-k with error <= N/k; KLL vs t-digest for quantiles. Libraries: Apache DataSketches (Java/C++/Python), Redis 8 probabilistic types, ClickHouse uniq* functions, PostgreSQL hll.

Similarity and dimension reduction: MinHash estimate error ~1/sqrt(k); LSH banding S-curve threshold ~(1/b)^(1/r); SimHash for cosine; Johnson-Lindenstrauss k >= 4 ln n/(eps^2/2 - eps^3/3); the datasketch library; verify exact similarity on candidate pairs.

Classic algorithms: randomised quickselect/quicksort; Karger min-cut (success >= 1/C(n,2) per run, so C(n,2) ln n repeats; Karger-Stein); Miller-Rabin with deterministic 64-bit bases {2,...,37}; Freivalds matrix-product check O(n^2), error <= 1/2 per round; Schwartz-Zippel identity testing (error <= d/|S|); treaps and skip lists; randomised rounding of LPs.

RNG engineering: seed and log every run; NumPy Generator (PCG64) with SeedSequence.spawn for parallel streams; xoshiro256** / PCG for simulation; never a non-cryptographic RNG for tokens (use secrets or the OS CSPRNG); expected bounds fail against adaptive adversaries who learn the seed.

Validation: run the sketch over >= 20 seeds and compare the empirical error distribution with the theoretical bound; test merges (same parameters and seeds required); property tests that a Bloom filter has no false negatives.

Worked example: 500M events/day. Hourly HLL p=14 sketches merged to daily distinct counts (~0.8% error). A 'seen before' Bloom filter for 50M keys at 0.1% FPR: 14.4 bits/key = 90 MB, k = 10. Empirical FPR checked across 20 seeds within the predicted band; plan for rotation when n exceeds capacity.

skills.name: concurrent-data-structures
skills.description: Correct shared-memory concurrency and lock-free data structures: data races vs race conditions, memory models (C++/Rust orderings, Java JMM and VarHandles, Go), linearizability and progress guarantees, lock design, CAS loops and ABA, safe memory reclamation (hazard pointers, epochs, RCU), standard designs (SPSC ring, Vyukov MPMC, Michael-Scott queue, Treiber stack, sharded counters), false sharing, and checking with TSan, loom, Shuttle, miri, jcstress, Lincheck and GenMC. Load when building, reviewing or debugging concurrent code.
outline: Decision ladder: avoid sharing (message passing, per-thread state, sharding); then a coarse lock; then striped or RW locks; then an existing library lock-free structure; custom lock-free code only as a last resort, and only with model checking.

Definitions kept from §10: a data race (UB in C/C++ and unsafe Rust) vs a race condition (bad interleaving); linearizability and naming a linearization point per operation; progress hierarchy wait-free > lock-free > obstruction-free > blocking (deadlock-free, starvation-free).

Memory-order table: Relaxed (counters only), Acquire/Release (publication and message passing), AcqRel (RMW), SeqCst (store-load ordering and Dekker-style flags); Java volatile and VarHandle modes (plain/opaque/acquire-release/volatile) and final-field semantics; Go sync/atomic is sequentially consistent. x86 TSO hides bugs that appear on ARM64 (Apple Silicon, Graviton), so test there.

Lock patterns: a global lock order against deadlock (the four Coffman conditions); lock striping; RW locks only for long read sections; seqlocks for small read-mostly data; correct lazy init (std::call_once, OnceLock/LazyLock, holder idiom) instead of hand-rolled double-checked locking; condition variables in a predicate loop; priority inversion; no lock held across await or I/O.

CAS loop template and ABA: the retry structure, with backoff under contention; ABA arises only with node reuse, so fix it with tagged pointers / version counters, DWCAS (cmpxchg16b), LL/SC, or by choosing a reclamation scheme. Garbage-collected runtimes avoid node-reuse ABA.

Safe memory reclamation comparison: hazard pointers (bounded garbage, per-access fence; C++26 <hazard_pointer>, folly), epoch-based (crossbeam-epoch: fast, but a stalled thread leaves garbage unbounded), RCU (liburcu, C++26 <rcu>, Linux), split reference counts and arc-swap. Lock-free without reclamation is a use-after-free.

Design catalogue with library picks: SPSC ring buffer (rtrb, boost::lockfree::spsc_queue, folly ProducerConsumerQueue), bounded MPMC with sequence numbers (Vyukov; crossbeam ArrayQueue), Michael-Scott queue (Java ConcurrentLinkedQueue), Treiber stack, LCRQ, concurrent maps (ConcurrentHashMap, DashMap, papaya, folly, libcuckoo), LongAdder / sharded counters, left-right and arc-swap for read-mostly snapshots.

False sharing: pad hot fields to 64 bytes, or 128 bytes on Apple M-series and Intel with adjacent-line prefetch (crossbeam CachePadded, std::hardware_destructive_interference_size, @Contended with -XX:-RestrictContended); measure with perf c2c.

Checking toolbox: ThreadSanitizer (clang/gcc -fsanitize=thread, go test -race, Rust -Zsanitizer=thread); loom (exhaustive with a preemption bound) and Shuttle (randomised PCT) for Rust; miri with -Zmiri-many-seeds; jcstress for JMM outcomes; Lincheck for Kotlin/Java linearizability; GenMC for C11 weak memory; Porcupine for linearizability of recorded histories; stress runs on ARM hardware.

Benchmarking concurrent structures: a throughput vs thread-count curve up to oversubscription, pinned threads, tail latency under contention, and the contention-collapse signature. Generic statistics are delegated to performance-optimization.

Pitfalls: a relaxed flag guarding non-atomic data; volatile used as synchronisation in C/C++; check-then-act on concurrent maps (use compute/entry/putIfAbsent); iterating while mutating; user-space spinlocks without backoff under preemption; std::atomic<shared_ptr> assumed lock-free (libstdc++ uses a spinlock).

Worked example: an SPSC ring buffer in Rust. The producer writes the slot and then tail.store(Release); the consumer does tail.load(Acquire) and then reads the slot. Prove the happens-before edge, show a loom test that reports the UnsafeCell race with Relaxed and passes with Acquire/Release, and benchmark padded vs unpadded head/tail.

skills.name: distributed-consensus-consistency
skills.description: Replication protocols and the guarantees they actually give: failure and timing models, FLP/CAP/PACELC, quorum arithmetic (2f+1, 3f+1, R+W>N, flexible Paxos), Raft and Multi-Paxos safety checklists and implementation bugs, reconfiguration, linearizable reads (ReadIndex, leases), fencing, the consistency-model hierarchy and session guarantees, clocks, CRDTs, idempotency/outbox/sagas, and testing with deterministic simulation and Jepsen/Elle/Porcupine. Load when designing, reviewing or debugging replicated state or a consistency claim.
outline: Model declaration table kept from the reference: timing (sync, partially synchronous, async), process failures (crash-stop, crash-recovery, omission, Byzantine), network (loss, duplication, reordering, partitions), clocks (none / NTP ms / bounded uncertainty), and storage (fsync honoured, torn writes).

Impossibility results and arithmetic: FLP; CAP vs PACELC; quorum formulas kept from the reference (n = 2f+1 with majority quorums; n = 3f+1 with 2f+1 quorums; R+W>N; flexible Paxos |Q1|+|Q2| > n); even n adds cost but no tolerance; commit latency = RTT to the median-fastest majority, with region placement rules.

Raft safety checklist kept from the reference (election restriction, current-term commit rule (Figure 8), fsync of term/vote/log before replying, single-server or joint-consensus membership changes, ReadIndex or lease reads, request-id dedup), plus frequent implementation bugs: missing pre-vote/check-quorum, snapshot install races, truncating committed entries, and an unpersisted votedFor.

Paxos family and alternatives: single-decree phases, Multi-Paxos with a distinguished leader, EPaxos, Viewstamped Replication, Zab; BFT (PBFT O(n^2), HotStuff linear view change) at n = 3f+1; chain replication; primary-backup needs fencing.

Use, don't write: production libraries etcd-io/raft (Go), hashicorp/raft, openraft and raft-rs (Rust), Apache Ratis (Java), NuRaft (C++); delegate coordination to etcd, ZooKeeper or Consul; a checklist for evaluating a library (Jepsen history, read semantics, snapshot support).

Consistency hierarchy kept from the reference (linearizable > sequential > causal > PRAM > eventual) plus session guarantees (RYW, monotonic reads/writes, writes-follow-reads), and a requirement -> minimum model -> mechanism table: plain R+W>N is not linearizable; ABD with write-back is; CRDTs give strong eventual consistency. Transactional isolation is delegated to database-transactions-isolation.

Time and ordering kept from the reference: Lamport, vector and dotted version vectors, HLC, bounded uncertainty with commit-wait ~2*eps, leases that are safe only under a drift bound, and a fencing-token procedure (storage rejects stale tokens) for GC pauses and VM migration.

CRDTs: semilattice laws (commutative, associative, idempotent merge), the type table kept from the reference (G/PN-counter, LWW and MV registers, OR-set, sequence CRDTs RGA/Fugue), delta-state CRDTs, libraries (Automerge, Yjs, Loro), and testing by random operation orders with duplicate delivery.

End-to-end effects: exactly-once effect = at-least-once delivery + idempotent processing; idempotency keys with a TTL beyond the retry horizon; the outbox pattern; sagas with explicit compensations and accepted anomalies; 2PC blocking and replicated coordinators. Retries and backoff are delegated to caching-and-system-tradeoffs.

Testing: deterministic simulation (FoundationDB style, TigerBeetle VOPR, Antithesis, madsim/turmoil for Rust); Jepsen nemeses (partitions, clock skew, pauses, disk faults); Knossos/Porcupine for linearizability and Elle for transactional anomalies; TLA+ spec plus trace validation (link to formal-verification-tla-dafny).

Pitfalls: 'exactly-once delivery'; leader leases without fencing; a majority quorum split across 2 regions; LWW with skewed clocks silently dropping writes; follower reads labelled linearizable; jumping between disjoint majorities on reconfiguration.

Worked example: review a 'follower reads' PR on a Raft KV store. Construct the stale-read history under a partition, then compare fixes (forward-to-leader ReadIndex at 1 RTT, follower ReadIndex as in etcd, lease reads with a stated drift bound, or a documented bounded-staleness API). Check a recorded history with Porcupine and state the guarantee in the API docs.

skills.name: compiler-construction
skills.description: Building language front ends and optimisers: lexing, grammar design and parser choice (recursive descent with Pratt precedence, LL/LR/LALR, PEG, GLR, tree-sitter, combinators), error recovery and diagnostics, lossless syntax trees, IR design and SSA construction, monotone dataflow frameworks, classic optimisation passes and phase ordering, instruction selection and register allocation, LLVM/MLIR/Cranelift workflows, and compiler testing. Load when writing a parser, DSL, interpreter or compiler pass, or explaining surprising codegen.
outline: Pipeline kept from §8 plus an architecture decision: tree-walking interpreter -> bytecode VM -> compile to an existing IR (LLVM, Cranelift, WebAssembly via wasm-encoder/Binaryen) -> custom backend, chosen by performance need, startup time and team size.

Parser choice table: hand-written recursive descent plus Pratt (Clang, rustc, Go, TypeScript); LALR (bison, lalrpop); ALL(*) (ANTLR 4); PEG (pest, peggy, CPython's pegen); GLR/Earley for ambiguous or incremental parsing (tree-sitter for editors); combinators (nom, chumsky, megaparsec).

Pratt parsing: a binding-power table, prefix/infix/postfix handlers, left vs right associativity via (l_bp, r_bp) pairs, ternary and call/index postfix forms, and a ~40-line skeleton with tests for precedence and associativity.

Grammar hygiene: remove left recursion for LL/PEG, left-factor, resolve dangling else, encode operator precedence; use bison -Wcounterexamples for conflicts; lexer modes for string interpolation, maximal munch, keyword-vs-identifier priority, DFA lexer generators (re2c, logos, flex).

Error recovery and diagnostics: panic-mode sync tokens, error productions, continuing to report multiple errors; span-carrying diagnostics (ariadne, miette, codespan-reporting); lossless CSTs (rowan, Roslyn-style red-green trees) for IDE and LSP features.

IR and SSA: three-address code, basic blocks, CFG; dominators (Cooper-Harvey-Kennedy iterative, Lengauer-Tarjan); phi placement at dominance frontiers (Cytron) vs Braun et al. on-the-fly SSA construction; pruned SSA; out-of-SSA copy insertion (lost-copy and swap problems).

Dataflow framework: lattice, meet, transfer function and direction, with a table (reaching definitions fwd/union, liveness bwd/union, available expressions fwd/intersection, very busy expressions bwd/intersection, constant-propagation lattice); worklist algorithm; termination by finite height or widening for intervals.

Optimisation pass catalogue with prerequisites and typical order: SCCP, GVN/CSE, DCE/ADCE, inlining heuristics, LICM, induction-variable simplification and strength reduction, unrolling, vectorisation, escape analysis / scalar replacement, tail calls, peephole rules; e-graphs and equality saturation (egg/egglog, Cranelift ISLE + aegraph); phase-ordering pitfalls.

Backend: instruction selection (tree pattern matching, SelectionDAG vs GlobalISel), register allocation (Chaitin-Briggs colouring with coalescing and spilling, linear scan for JITs, chordal SSA graphs), scheduling and calling conventions; the UB lens for C/C++ codegen surprises.

Tooling commands kept and extended: Compiler Explorer; clang -O2 -S -emit-llvm; opt -passes='default<O2>' with -print-after-all / -print-changed; -Rpass and -Rpass-missed; llvm-mca; rustc --emit=llvm-ir,mir; mlir-opt with dialect pipelines; Cranelift via Wasmtime.

Compiler testing: FileCheck/lit-style golden tests, snapshot tests (insta), differential testing against a reference interpreter, random program generators (Csmith, YARPGen), grammar-aware fuzzing (cargo-fuzz, AFL++), Alive2 to validate peephole rewrites, and translation validation.

Worked example: add SCCP to a toy SSA IR. Define the 3-level lattice, run the dual worklists over SSA edges and CFG edges, fold a branch on a constant and delete the unreachable block, golden-test the output, and compare with opt -passes=sccp on equivalent LLVM IR.

skills.name: type-systems-inference
skills.description: Type system design and inference for language and tooling work: soundness via progress and preservation, Hindley-Milner unification with level-based generalisation and the value restriction, bidirectional checking, subtyping and variance, generics (monomorphisation, erasure, dictionaries), traits/type classes and coherence, substructural and ownership types, effects, refinement and dependent types, gradual typing, implementation techniques, and debugging hard type errors in real checkers. Load when designing a checker, writing inference, judging soundness, or untangling a type error.
outline: Concept table kept from §7 (soundness, HM, System F, variance, bidirectional, linear/affine, dependent, effects, gradual, refinement), with one-line consequences for each.

Soundness workflow: syntax-directed typing rules, canonical forms, the substitution lemma, then progress + preservation; mechanise small calculi in Lean 4, Agda or Rocq, or prototype in PLT Redex; state soundness relative to a given operational semantics.

HM inference procedure: constraint generation, unification with occurs check over union-find type variables, generalisation at let using levels (Remy/OCaml) instead of scanning the environment, instantiation at use sites, value restriction / relaxed value restriction for references. Worst case is exponential with nested lets but near-linear in practice. Includes a 30-line unify skeleton.

Bidirectional typing: check vs infer modes, the annotation rule, subsumption; why it scales to higher-rank types and GADTs; a sketch of the Dunfield-Krishnaswami 'complete and easy' algorithm; where annotations are required.

Subtyping and variance: covariant producers, contravariant consumers and function arguments, invariant mutable containers; declaration-site variance (Kotlin out/in, Scala +/-) vs use-site (Java wildcards, PECS); structural vs nominal typing; TypeScript method bivariance and strictFunctionTypes; Java array covariance and ArrayStoreException.

Polymorphism implementations: parametric vs ad hoc vs subtype; monomorphisation (Rust, C++; code size and compile time) vs erasure (Java, Kotlin; reified inline functions) vs dictionary passing (Haskell); higher-kinded types; trait/type-class coherence and orphan rules; associated types, type families and GADTs.
Substructural and ownership types: linear (exactly once), affine (at most once: Rust moves), uniqueness, regions/lifetimes, Rust NLL and Polonius borrow checking, session types for protocols.

Effects, refinement and dependent types: algebraic effects (OCaml 5, Koka, Effekt) and effect rows; refinement checking via SMT (Liquid Haskell, F*, Flux for Rust); dependent types (Lean 4, Agda, Idris 2) and why type checking needs termination checking.

Gradual and practical checkers: TypeScript (unsound by design: any, bivariance, satisfies, conditional/mapped types), Python checkers (mypy, pyright/basedpyright, ty, pyrefly), Sorbet; a catalogue of soundness holes (TS any, Java raw types, Kotlin platform types, unchecked casts).

Implementation techniques: de Bruijn indices or locally nameless binders, union-find unification with path compression, an elaborator producing a typed core IR, error messages with expected/actual and provenance; testing by generating well-typed terms (property-based) and differential checks against a reference checker.

Debugging hard type errors: minimise the snippet; add annotations to localise where unification fails; ask the checker for inferred types (GHCi :t and typed holes, reveal_type in mypy/pyright, the Rust let () = x; trick, TS twoslash // ^?); recognise variance and implicit-conversion causes.

Worked example: infer compose = fun f -> fun g -> fun x -> f (g x) step by step (constraints, unifier, generalisation) to ('b -> 'c) -> ('a -> 'b) -> 'a -> 'c; then show why let r = ref [] must not be generalised (value restriction) using a two-line unsoundness counterexample.

skills.name: formal-verification-tla-dafny
skills.description: Formal verification in practice: choosing the tool (TLA+ with TLC/Apalache, PlusCal, P, Alloy 6, Z3/cvc5, CBMC, Kani, Dafny, Verus, Lean 4), writing specs with complete actions, environment models, invariants and fairness, bounding and symmetry, vacuity checks, refinement and trace validation, verified functions with loop invariants, bounded model checking harnesses, and reporting results with their bounds. Load when a protocol, design or function must be shown correct beyond testing.
outline: Tool-choice table kept from the reference, with cost per question (hours vs days vs weeks). When formal methods pay off: concurrency, distributed protocols, security-critical parsers, money and ledger invariants, and repeated production incidents in one subsystem.

Workflow kept from §11: state + actions -> safety invariants (TypeOK + property) -> small configurations with symmetry -> liveness with explicit fairness -> counterexample trace turned into a regression test -> trace validation of implementation logs against the spec.

TLA+ skeleton kept verbatim (Counter.tla + .cfg finding the lost update) with run commands: tlc2.TLC -workers auto, -simulate for random exploration of big specs, -coverage to find dead actions; Apalache check --length with type annotations; the VS Code TLA+ extension.

Spec-writing rules kept from the reference: every variable primed or UNCHANGED; explicit environment actions for loss, duplication, crash and clock drift; a CONSTRAINT to keep state finite; SYMMETRY only for safety (never liveness); WF/SF fairness; a deliberately false invariant as a vacuity check; refinement mappings to an abstract spec.
Replication invariants kept (ElectionSafety, LogMatching, StateMachineSafety with a Min helper) as templates, cross-linked to distributed-consensus-consistency.

Dafny: the verified Max example kept; a recipe for finding loop invariants (replace a constant in the postcondition with the loop variable, add bounds); decreases clauses, ghost state, lemmas, opaque functions; --resource-limit and assertion splitting for brittle proofs; compiling to Go/Java/C#/Python/JS; Verus as the Rust counterpart.

SMT directly: the Z3 Python pattern prove(claim) = check unsat(Not(claim)); bit-vector vs integer semantics (overflow is visible only in BitVec); quantifier triggers and timeouts; cvc5 as a cross-check; example proving a bit-trick equivalence and refuting (a+b)/2 for 32-bit ints.

Bounded model checking: the Kani midpoint harness kept, plus #[kani::unwind], experimental function contracts (kani::requires/ensures) and cargo kani --harness; CBMC with --bounds-check --pointer-check --unwind N --unwinding-assertions; always report the unwind bound.

Other modelling tools: Alloy 6 (relational plus temporal operators) for data models and access policies; the P language for event-driven services; loom/Shuttle via concurrent-data-structures; Lean 4 + Mathlib for mathematical lemmas (link to mathematics-toolkit).

Reporting template kept (artifact, properties, bounds, result with state counts and time, vacuity, not covered, status), using the status line 'model-checked within bounds, not a proof for all sizes' when that is the case.

Pitfalls: vacuous specs or an over-constrained Init; unrealistic fairness assumptions; an abstraction gap between spec and code; assume or {:verify false} left in final Dafny; unbounded quantifiers timing out and being read as success; a spec that silently drifts from the code.

Worked example: the Counter lost update (p1 and p2 both read 0) found by TLC. Fix it in the spec with an atomic increment or a lock variable, re-check with state counts reported, run the vacuity check, then port the fix to code with a regression test that replays the trace.

skills.name: caching-and-system-tradeoffs
skills.description: Caching and systems-design trade-offs backed by numbers: cache placement and write policies, eviction (LRU, LFU, ARC, W-TinyLFU, SIEVE, S3-FIFO), hit-ratio math and miss-ratio curves, TTL and invalidation, stampede protection, cache consistency races, partitioning (consistent, rendezvous, jump, Maglev hashing), fan-out tail latency, queueing (Little's law, utilisation knee), backpressure, retries with budgets, rate limiting, and decision records. Load when adding or debugging a cache or justifying a design trade-off quantitatively.
outline: Trade-off framing: name the axes (latency, throughput, consistency, cost, durability, availability, operability), the workload (read/write ratio, Zipf skew s, object sizes, peak QPS) and the SLOs; write each decision as 'accept X to gain Y, measured by Z', with reversibility noted. Latency constants and benchmarking are delegated to performance-optimization.

Back-of-envelope procedure: bandwidth = QPS x size; working set and growth; Little's law L = lambda*W; M/M/1 W = 1/(mu - lambda) with the knee at 70-80% utilisation; fan-out tail P(any slow) = 1 - p^n (100 calls at p99 -> 63% of requests touch a slow call); hedged requests and their cost.

Cache pattern table: cache-aside, read-through, write-through, write-behind, refresh-ahead, each with its consistency risk; tiers (in-process near cache, Valkey/Redis/Memcached, CDN with Cache-Control/ETag/stale-while-revalidate, the DB buffer pool); what must never be cached (authorisation decisions without an invalidation path).

Eviction policy table: LRU, CLOCK, LFU, ARC, LIRS, W-TinyLFU (Caffeine, moka, Ristretto), SIEVE (2024), S3-FIFO (2023), Redis approximate LRU/LFU (maxmemory-samples); choose by scan resistance and frequency skew; replay real traces with libCacheSim before choosing.

Hit-ratio and sizing math: effective latency = h*t_hit + (1-h)*t_miss; backend load = (1-h)*QPS, so 99% -> 99.9% cuts backend load 10x; miss-ratio curves via SHARDS sampling; the Che approximation; measure byte and cost hit ratios, not only request hit ratio.

TTL and invalidation: TTL jitter of +/-10-20% against synchronised expiry; CDC-driven invalidation (Debezium -> key deletes); versioned / generation keys; short-TTL negative caching; key design (tenant, schema version, locale, normalised parameters; bounded cardinality).

Stampede protection: single-flight request coalescing (Go singleflight, Caffeine async loaders); probabilistic early expiration (XFetch: recompute when now - delta*beta*ln(rand()) >= expiry); stale-while-revalidate; memcache-style leases; warm-up after deploys or flushes.

Cache consistency races: the read-old-DB / invalidate / write-stale-cache interleaving and its fixes (leases, versioned compare-and-set, delete-after-commit with a delayed second delete, TTL as a safety net); read-your-writes via write-through or bypass for the writer.

Partitioning and hot keys: mod-N rehashing moves (N-1)/N of keys; consistent hashing with ~100-200 virtual nodes; rendezvous (HRW) hashing; jump consistent hash (no arbitrary removals); Maglev; hot-key mitigation by local caching, key splitting or replication.

Cache-specific degradation (timeouts, retries with jitter, breakers and rate limits live in resilience-patterns): serve stale on backend errors, short-TTL negative caching, load shedding when the cache tier is down, bounded refill concurrency after a flush.

Pitfalls: caches without eviction; caching errors or nulls forever; the cache as source of truth; unbounded key cardinality; serialisation cost dominating the hit path; cold start after flush; hit ratio measured on the wrong denominator; cache-only correctness assumptions during an outage.

Worked example: a product-page service at 20k RPS whose DB sustains 2k QPS (1.4k at 70% headroom) needs a hit ratio >= 93%. Design an in-process W-TinyLFU tier for 10k hot items plus a Valkey cluster, TTL 5 min +/-15%, CDC invalidation and singleflight; validate with a miss-ratio curve from a sampled trace; plan the Valkey-down mode with load shedding; write it up as an ADR.

skills.name: database-transactions-isolation
skills.description: How databases store, version and isolate data: B+tree vs LSM engines, WAL and recovery, MVCC and vacuum, row locks and SKIP LOCKED queues, real vendor isolation semantics, anomalies as concrete histories, and fixes with constraints or retries. Load when concurrent transactions misbehave, picking an isolation level, or reasoning about storage engines (query tuning lives in sql-query-tuning).
outline: Scope split: index design and plan reading live in sql-query-tuning, DDL lock levels in zero-downtime-migrations; this skill covers how the engine stores, versions and isolates rows.

Storage engines: B+tree vs leveled/tiered LSM vs Bitcask vs columnar with read/write/space amplification (RUM); page sizes (PostgreSQL 8 KB, InnoDB 16 KB); heap vs clustered tables, InnoDB secondaries carrying the PK, UUIDv7 (PG18 uuidv7()) over random v4 keys.
Durability: WAL, checkpoints, ARIES analysis/redo/undo with steal/no-force, fsync semantics, torn pages (full_page_writes, doublewrite buffer), group commit and synchronous_commit trade-offs.

MVCC: PostgreSQL tuple versions (xmin/xmax), visibility rules, HOT updates and fillfactor, VACUUM/autovacuum tuning, xid wraparound, bloat; InnoDB undo logs and purge; long transactions blocking cleanup; replica lag and hot_standby_feedback.

Locking: row locks (FOR UPDATE, FOR NO KEY UPDATE, FOR SHARE), SKIP LOCKED job queues, advisory locks, deadlock detection and consistent lock order, lock_timeout/statement_timeout; reading pg_locks and pg_stat_activity.

Isolation with real vendor semantics: PostgreSQL REPEATABLE READ = snapshot isolation and SERIALIZABLE = SSI (retry on SQLSTATE 40001); InnoDB REPEATABLE READ with next-key locks and current-data locking reads; Oracle SERIALIZABLE = SI; SQL Server RCSI/SNAPSHOT; CockroachDB SERIALIZABLE by default.
Anomaly catalogue as interleaved histories (dirty read, non-repeatable read, lost update, read skew, write skew, phantom, read-only anomaly) and which level prevents each per vendor.

Fix menu: SERIALIZABLE plus a bounded retry loop with idempotent bodies, SELECT ... FOR UPDATE, unique or exclusion constraints, materialised conflict rows, atomic conditional UPDATE ... WHERE stock >= 1 RETURNING.

Reproduce before fixing: two-session psql scripts, pgbench custom scripts with concurrency, the Hermitage suite as reference behaviour; Elle-style history checking (distributed-consensus-consistency).

Pitfalls: trusting the ORM's default isolation, read-modify-write in application code, SERIALIZABLE without retries, retries that repeat non-idempotent side effects, assuming REPEATABLE READ means the same thing across vendors.

Worked example: inventory oversell (lost update) and on-call write skew reproduced under READ COMMITTED and REPEATABLE READ in PostgreSQL, fixed with an atomic conditional UPDATE and with SERIALIZABLE + retry; retry rate measured under pgbench.
